title: 4.4 WHEELING POWER
summary: The Wheeling Power chapter examines how electricity actually moves between regions and what that means for trading long-distance price differences. It starts from the physical layer — AC transmission losing power as the square of current, transformers stepping voltage via magnetic induction, and power routing along paths of least resistance rather than intended contracts — then builds up to how HVDC offers a lower-loss but less flexible alternative for long hauls, and the broader trade-offs (losses, failure points, siting constraints) that shape investment in these links. It then connects this physical picture to the economics: since regional prices are typically set by the marginal generator, and a price spread is just one region's price minus another's, transmission constraints and physics create the divergences that a location spread trade can exploit, illustrated with a worked NP-15/MID-C example. A closing note on regulation covers why transmission rental pricing on shared lines is typically kept nondiscriminatory rather than competitive.
provenance: rewritten orientation from this chapter's concept set; no new claims
